newsitem.title: USA: MCI takes on Baby Bells in America's rural heartland.
newsitem.headline: MCI takes on Baby Bells in America's rural heartland.

text.p: MCI Communications Corp. on Thursday threw down the gauntlet to the Baby Bells with the launch of a venture to bring competitive local phone services, entertainment and Internet services to rural America.

MCI is teaming up with Northwest Iowa Power Cooperative and Northwest Iowa Telephone, which is a unit of Long Lines Ltd, to form Pioneer Holdings LLC, which will begin by serving rural communities in Iowa.
Though it is a small beginning, the partners said they are negotiating with around 300 municipalities and other entities in 10 states.
"MCI is breaking new ground with this initiative," said John Gerdelman, president of networkMCI Services. "It is a model we hope to replicate throughout the country."
MCI said they would add new power company and local phone company partners as they expand the service into new areas.
The effort is a blow to regional Bells, which assumed they would keep a grip on rural customers long after they are fighting tooth and nail to keep big city customers and business users.
It is also a potential threat to satellite television companies, which assumed they would have the rural entertainment market to themselves.
"There is more than one way to skin this rural cat," said consultant Debra McMahon of Mercer Management Consulting.
Sources close to the deal first disclosed it to Reuters late on Wednesday.
U S West Communications and GTE Corp. have local calling regions in Iowa.

The MCI service will use a hybrid fiber coaxial cable system to reach neighbourhoods and the latest technologies for squeezing data into existing cables for the last few hundred yards to the home. Service will begin in the summer.

The cable modems to decode the data will be made either by privately owned Comm 21 Inc. or by Motorola Inc., according to information contained on a website of one of the participants, consultancy TeleChoice Inc.
3Com Corp. owns a stake in Comm 21.
Other companies involved include Westell Technologies Inc., Internet company Pioneer ISP, Northern Telecom Ltd, PairGain Technologies Inc. Performance Telecom and NEC Corp..
No figures on MCI's investment were disclosed. A spokeswoman said it would depend on how broadly the service was implemented.

Analysts have predicted that competition for local calling services, made possible in the 1996 Telecommunications Act, will materialise only slowly in rural areas, where it is expensive to lay new phone lines and residents are spread out.
But power companies, which have fiberoptic cables alongside their powerlines into communities, could change that and enter a profitable new business, too.
McMahon said that while some rural areas were poor or technologically conservative, there was a pent-up demand for video entertainment and Internet services in many areas.

Industry studies say rural residents could be among the heaviest potential users of Internet commerce, just as they were mail order pioneers, because many are tens of miles away from the nearest big city stores.
"These could be very lucrative pocket franchises," McMahon said, adding that in many cases there would be no incentive for additional companies to compete for these customers.
MCI is not the only long distance services company looking to circumvent the Bells' grip on rural and suburban local calling markets.
Last month AT&T Corp. announced a fast wireless system it was developing to provide local and long distance calling, and high speed Internet access to some local areas.
